paras: The threatened lynching of George Crisp was a series of threats in March and May 1888 by residents of Coal Hill, Arkansas, a mining camp, to lynch Crisp, who was jailed at Ozark charged with criminal assault on the eight-year-old daughter of a Coal Hill minister. In March a St. Louis dispatch forecast "a double lynching" of Crisp and of Clifford, a penitentiary warden accused of brutality to convicts. In May about thirty armed men seized a switch engine to go to Ozark for Crisp, but the party broke up in a dispute before leaving, and no report says Crisp was harmed.

In mid-March 1888, dispatches from St. Louis and Little Rock described the abuse of convicts leased to work the Coal Hill mines, near Fort Smith. A "colored convict" named Williams was reported flogged to death, and other prisoners were said to have been beaten or kicked to death, one of them by a fellow convict "egged on" by Warden Grafford. The citizens of Coal Hill were described as "much excited," threatening to hang the warden and "tear down the prison barracks." By March 21 the dispatches named the warden as Clifford, "the penitentiary warden who so brutally served the prisoners under him."

On March 21 a special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported that the people of Coal Hill were "worked up to a furor" over a series of outrages and that a double lynching was promised "very soon." According to the special, Clifford was in the sheriff's hands and was to be taken to the Coal Hill jail, while the townspeople clamored for George Crisp, whom the sheriff had arrested the day before and lodged in the Ozark jail. Crisp was charged with criminal assault on the eight-year-old daughter of the Rev. Mr. Huddleston of Coal Hill; the Wheeling versions of the dispatch gave the minister's name as Turner. Both prisoners were "hourly expected at Coal Hill," the dispatch said, and "a hanging bee is very probable." A separate Little Rock brief of the same date said the two men were in jail at Coal Hill "and in danger of being lynched."

In May an Arkansas state-news column reported that about thirty armed men had organized at Coal Hill "a few nights ago" to go to Ozark and lynch Crisp. The men took possession of the switch engine, forced the engineer into service and boarded, but "a disagreement as to leaders and methods, it is said, broke the thing up in confusion."

No report of Crisp's trial, or of arrests for the attempt on him, appears in the coverage. The warden's case was followed further: in November J. A. Clifford, "a fugitive from justice since last March," was reported captured at Cumberland Gap, Tennessee, under indictment for the murder of convicts at Coal Hill. In December the warden was reported convicted of second-degree murder at Clarksville on one count and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary.

The March threat reached readers far from Arkansas mainly through the Post-Dispatch special, which the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and both Wheeling dailies printed on March 22. The Gazette headlined it "Hanging Bee Probable" over the line "An Arkansas Mining Camp Obtains an Unenviable Criminal Notoriety," while the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer used "A Hanging Bee Anticipated." The Wheeling Register's headline spoke of "Two Brutal Murderers," although Crisp was charged with assault, not murder. These texts treated the lynching as a forecast and did not criticize it.

The Ohio Democrat carried the Little Rock version on March 31 under the heading "In Danger of Being Lynched." The failed May expedition appeared only as a single paragraph among other Arkansas news items in the Osceola Times. None of the reports gave Crisp's race.

The reports differ on where the prisoners were held: the Post-Dispatch special placed Crisp in the Ozark jail, while the Little Rock brief put both men in jail at Coal Hill. The May report, in which the armed men set out for Ozark, supports the Ozark version. The March dispatches said Clifford was in the sheriff's hands, but the November report described him as a fugitive since March.

No report says Crisp was killed; the March threats were forecasts of a 'double lynching' (A3, A6), and the May party of about thirty armed men broke up before setting out (A7). It was a threatened lynching over a crime accusation.
The March threat appears in a St. Louis special (A3, A4) and in a separate Little Rock brief (A6), and the May attempt in an Arkansas state-news column (A7); none denies them.

framing.detail: The Fort Worth Daily Gazette headlined 'HANGING BEE PROBABLE' and described a 'peaceful mining camp' given a 'disgusting' criminal notoriety, without criticizing the expected lynching.
The Wheeling Register headlined 'A HANGING BEE / Expected When Two Brutal Murderers Reach Coal Hill', calling Crisp a murderer though he was charged with assault.
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran the same special as 'A Hanging Bee Anticipated'.
The Ohio Democrat ran a two-line Little Rock brief headed 'In Danger of Being Lynched.'
The Osceola Times reported the failed May expedition as one item in its Arkansas state news, with the breakup attributed to 'a disagreement as to leaders and methods'.
